Weird 'potato chips' and 'ghostly rocks' on Mars spotted by NASA rovers Curiosity and Perseverance

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (643 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • NASA's Curiosity and Perseverance rovers have spotted a bizarre assortment of Martian oddities, from potato chip-like rocks and ghostly white formations to mysterious patterns etched into the Red Planet's surface.
  • While their appearances may be unusual, these formations offer scientists something far more valuable than a collection of curious snapshots: clues to the geological processes that shaped Mars over billions of years.
  • In particular, the rocks and mineral deposits could help researchers piece together the planet's watery past and identify environments that may once have been capable of supporting microbial life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA's Curiosity and Perseverance rovers have spotted a bizarre assortment of Martian oddities, from potato chip-like rocks and ghostly white formations to mysterious patterns etched into the Red Planet's surface.

While their appearances may be unusual, these formations offer scientists something far more valuable than a collection of curious snapshots: clues to the geological processes that shaped Mars over billions of years.

In particular, the rocks and mineral deposits could help researchers piece together the planet's watery past and identify environments that may once have been capable of supporting microbial life.

NASA's Curiosity rover recently wrapped up a drilling campaign at a location nicknamed "Nazca," where scientists have been examining unusual disk-shaped crystal formations embedded in the surrounding bedrock. Some of the features are so thin and flat that the mission team likened them to potato chips, according to a statement from the space agency.

Curiosity used its Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI), mounted on the end of its robotic arm, to capture detailed close-up images of the formations on Nov. 7 — the rover's 5,067th Martian day, or Sol 5067. The rover also used its ChemCam instrument to study the rocks' chemical composition, while samples from the Nazca drill site were delivered to its onboard Sample Analysis at Mars (SAM) instrument for further analysis.

Meanwhile, NASA's Perseverance rover has been investigating a collection of unusually bright rocks in an area called "Idubi," located in the “Lac de Charmes” region outside Jezero Crater. The rover captured images of the formations on Oct. 29, 2026 (Sol 2023), revealing pale, ghostly-looking rocks that stand out dramatically against the darker, dust-covered Martian landscape.

Data from Perseverance's SuperCam instrument revealed that the rocks are rich in hydrated silica rather than being typical igneous rocks. That discovery has scientists particularly interested. On Earth, hydrated silica can form in environments involving hydrothermal activity or groundwater. These deposits are also capable of preserving microscopic fossils, making them valuable targets in the search for evidence of ancient life, according to another statement from NASA.

Perseverance is now conducting a closer investigation of the formations, using its instruments to gather detailed chemical and mineralogical data that could help scientists determine how the rocks formed and whether they preserve potential signs of past microbial activity.

Back at Mount Sharp, Curiosity has also spotted another geological curiosity: the return of distinctive polygon-shaped patterns across the Martian bedrock.

According to recent reports, the rover's latest images, captured on Nov. 13, 2026 (Sol 5073), show small, regularly shaped polygons outlined by raised ridges, resembling patterns the rover encountered earlier in its climb up the layered mountain, whose rocky slopes preserve a record of Mars' changing climate and ancient watery environments. Scientists say these formations could have developed through several processes, including mineral shrinkage as water evaporated, temperature changes or the expansion and compaction of buried sediments, according to a statement from NASA.

By studying the composition of the rocks and the material cementing the raised ridges around the polygons, researchers hope to determine which processes shaped the terrain.

Recent findings suggest that together, these discoveries highlight how much Mars' seemingly barren landscape can reveal about its past. As Curiosity continues climbing Mount Sharp and Perseverance investigates ancient terrain beyond Jezero Crater, both rovers are helping piece together the planet's unique features and complex geological history.

Previously, her work has been published in Nature World News. When not writing or reading about science, Samantha enjoys traveling to new places and taking photos! A material just one atom thick reveals a strange quantum secret

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (534 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that scientists at the University of Osaka in Japan have made a significant discovery in quantum physics, directly observing an unusual electronic state forming where a material just one atom thick meets a metal.
  • Recent findings suggest that to investigate this behavior, the researchers produced a carefully controlled, single atomic layer of ytterbium and copper (YbCu2) on the surface of a copper crystal.
  • The experiments uncovered two separate heavy fermion states with different characteristics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that scientists at the University of Osaka in Japan have made a significant discovery in quantum physics, directly observing an unusual electronic state forming where a material just one atom thick meets a metal. Known as a heavy fermion state, this phenomenon causes electrons to behave as though they have much greater mass than normal. These states are associated with extraordinary quantum effects, including unconventional superconductivity, and the discovery could provide a newly introduced way to develop materials with unusual electronic properties.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate this behavior, the researchers produced a carefully controlled, single atomic layer of ytterbium and copper (YbCu2) on the surface of a copper crystal. They then used powerful synchrotron light to study the electrons and their interactions at the boundary between the two materials. The results indicated that electrons confined to the thin atomic layer could interact with freely moving electrons in the copper beneath it, producing the unusual heavy fermion behavior.

Two Distinct Quantum States Emerge.

The experiments uncovered two separate heavy fermion states with different characteristics. One existed primarily within the two-dimensional atomic layer, while the other reached beyond that layer and into the three-dimensional copper crystal below.

According to recent reports, the second state was particularly important because it provided the first direct evidence of heavy fermion behavior generated by interactions across such an interface. Researchers traced the effect to the mixing, or hybridization, of localized ytterbium 4f electrons in the atomic layer with mobile conduction electrons inside the copper substrate. This interaction demonstrated how combining materials with different electronic characteristics can produce quantum behavior that neither material would necessarily exhibit on its own.

"This achievement was made possible by our continued efforts to create high-quality materials and measure their electronic states as precisely as possible," says senior author Professor Shin-ichi Kimura. "Our next goal is to engineer and control such heavy-electron states, opening the way to previously unexplored quantum states, including unconventional superconductivity.".

A New Approach to Designing Quantum Materials.

The discovery suggests that the boundaries between materials could become powerful tools for creating and controlling exotic quantum states. Rather than relying only on the properties of individual substances, scientists may be able to develop entirely new electronic behaviors by carefully selecting and combining ultrathin atomic layers with suitable underlying materials.

According to recent reports, future research could focus on adjusting the structures of these interfaces, controlling the electronic orbitals involved, and manipulating moiré patterns that arise when atomic arrangements overlap. Such approaches may allow researchers to produce and fine-tune quantum phenomena in materials with extremely small dimensions, including effects that cannot be achieved in conventional materials. Ultimately, this could open newly introduced possibilities for engineering advanced quantum materials and investigating unconventional superconductivity.

Centuries-old dust hints at a dying stars last-minute chaos

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (724 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The mix of elements that ends up in planets — even people — can hinge on a final shake-up inside a dying star, new space observations suggest.
  • Sources indicate that A team of researchers studied Cassiopeia A, a glowing cloud of gas and dust left behind by an exploding star.
  • "What's amazing is that the dust, which we are testing hundreds of years after the explosion, tells us about what happened to the star potentially only hours before it exploded," remarked Dan Milisavljevic, a Purdue University professor and co-author of the study, in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The mix of elements that ends up in planets — even people — can hinge on a final shake-up inside a dying star, new space observations suggest.

Sources indicate that A team of researchers studied Cassiopeia A, a glowing cloud of gas and dust left behind by an exploding star. Using NASA's James Webb Space Telescope, the astronomers could parse out clumps within the 350-year-old cloud and analyze their compositions. The debris from the explosion, called a supernova, is still racing outward in space at about 11 million mph.

"What's amazing is that the dust, which we are testing hundreds of years after the explosion, tells us about what happened to the star potentially only hours before it exploded," remarked Dan Milisavljevic, a Purdue University professor and co-author of the study, in a statement.

Supernova explosions forge and scatter many of the heavy elements that later get recycled into upcoming stars and worlds. Computer models have long predicted that a star's inner layers could merge before it explodes. But scientists don't fully understand why and how some stars go through this violent process. The new study, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, adds evidence that it happened in Cassiopeia A, giving astronomers a way to peer inside a star that hasn't existed for centuries.

It has been revealed that A massive star builds up in layers, like an onion, with each shell fusing a different element. When the star explodes, some of that material cools into dust. Each layer makes its own kind of dust, so the grains, smaller than the width of a human hair, keep a record of what sat where inside the star.

As the layers merge, they can change the mix of elements the blast flings out, remarked Tea Temim, lead author of the study.

Recent findings suggest that "So, for example, the oxygen- and carbon-burning shells in a star merge together and change the structure of the star significantly," remarked Temim, a research scientist at Columbia University in New York. "And that would then change the chemical abundances that you would see after a supernova explosion.".

To look for evidence, the team pointed Webb at three spots in Cassiopeia A, or Cas A, that NASA's retired Spitzer Space Telescope had previously flagged. Spitzer saw the debris as a blur, with light from many clumps mixed together. Webb's sharper view separates individual clumps, each roughly the size of our solar system, so the team could study them one at a time.

Recent findings suggest that one clump held mostly silica dust, the main ingredient in most sand. Another held mostly carbon dust. The third sits in a feature nicknamed the Green Monster, and its dust is rich in magnesium and silicon. That material didn't come from the blast at all; rather, the star shed it before it exploded.

According to recent reports, the researchers then compared their measurements with existing computer models of exploding stars. Only the models in which the star's layers had merged could reproduce both the silica-rich and the carbon-rich debris. A wider Webb dust map shows signs of the merger across much of the cloud.

The team cautions that those models are incomplete. Researchers will need more detailed 3D simulations — and Webb observations of more spots in the cloud — to confirm the merger.

This approach also could help astronomers make sense of supernovas in other galaxies.

"I think it's remarkable that we can watch these changes and understand what they mean from thousands of light-years away," Milisavljevic stated.

#116651. Industry News: Inside the Chinese City Where Furniture Dupes Are Made

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 23m • 📚 Deep Dive (4661 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Inside the Chinese City Where Furniture Dupes Are Made

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4661 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, on the morning of May 31, 2025, Shirley Bekker made an impulsive decision.
  • According to recent reports, two months prior, Bekker had little knowledge of the city of 9 million; she had no idea what hotel to stay at or where to go once she landed.
  • Recent findings suggest that bekker was in the process of buying her dream one-bedroom apartment in East London and spent weeks obsessively watching home renovation videos on TikTok.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, on the morning of May 31, 2025, Shirley Bekker made an impulsive decision. The then 29-year-old doctor living in London finally pulled the trigger on plane tickets to visit Foshan, in southern China, for a flight later that same day.

According to recent reports, two months prior, Bekker had little knowledge of the city of 9 million; she had no idea what hotel to stay at or where to go once she landed. But Bekker was convinced that six days in Foshan to furnish her apartment—and possibly having all of the furniture shipped back to London—would still be cheaper than getting everything at home. With over 100,000 followers on social media, she also later turned her adventure into content, detailing her finds and their cost.

Recent findings suggest that bekker was in the process of buying her dream one-bedroom apartment in East London and spent weeks obsessively watching home renovation videos on TikTok. “When I saw that things like a sofa cost thousands of pounds, I was like, ‘OK, I’m convinced now that I’ll probably do something drastic to not have to pay that much,’” she says. Her social media algorithm was already feeding her a radical solution. “Made in China, shit quality?” a Chinese furniture seller remarked in videos on Bekker’s TikTok feed. “Grass sofa? Our factory has mass-produced it; UFO table? Our factory has mass-produced it.” Soon, Bekker says, her “entire timeline became Foshan, Foshan, Foshan.” She learned all about China’s furniture capital, which each year exports nearly $10 billion worth of couches and beds and bathroom vanities, and everything else you could possibly need for your home.

Industry observers note that bekker is just one of a growing number of people around the world who order furniture directly from factories in Foshan. By either flying to the city—or through WhatsApp, TikTok, AliExpress, or Alibaba—buyers can commission made-to-order pieces. And most importantly, they can purchase dupes.

In 2025, Shirley Bekker flew to China to buy furniture, hoping that even with shipping the cost would be lower than shopping in London.

Industry observers note that duplicates were once primarily the domain of fashion and beauty, but consumers are now seeking out knockoffs of luxury designer furniture that promise the same quality as the original at a much lower cost—even after international shipping rates and tariffs. During the week of April 13, 2025, the number of videos urging Americans to buy directly from Chinese factories soared 250 percent. Tens of thousands of videos had been posted under hashtags like #ChineseFactory, and many of them were about furniture pieces. Some videos garnered millions of views and included contacts of Chinese sellers in the comments.

@gabwithmeg, a working mom in California, claims on TikTok that she saved at least $100,000 by furnishing her entire house directly from China. “It is all Restoration Hardware and Arhaus-style furniture, and I’m going to tell you exactly how I did it,” she promised her followers in January. @gabwithmeg’s post received over 65,000 likes, and the comments are filled with users clamoring to opt out of the traditional furniture market, if not bragging about having already done so.

Together, they represent a turning tide in furniture shopping for Westerners. If people can buy a couch that looks exactly like the famous Togo for $200 on AliExpress, why would they pay $4,800 for one from Design Within Reach? Sure, Ligne Roset is a legendary brand, famously crafting all its furniture near the French Alps, made by trained artisans using an almost entirely manual process. But not everyone cares about history, owning an original, or the ethics of intellectual property in design. In fact, some furniture buyers, including Bekker, aren’t even aware that some pieces they covet are copies. Bekker feels that designer furniture is more expensive because of the brand name, not necessarily the quality. “Sorry to say, for me, it’s a bit bullshit,” she says. “I’m really not one to buy into the idea that the name of the brand makes it worth the price.”.

“We’re seeing the beginnings of a revolt against the brandification of everything,” claims Christopher Sprigman, a law professor at Latest York University who has studied the knockoff economy. As a consumer, Sprigman expects brands to offer good and consistent quality, but there is a perception that “there’s no real quality control, there’s no real integrity, it’s basically just advertising and driving up costs, creating demand, creating desire without any real substantial benefit that the consumer can feel or taste or see,” Sprigman says.

In a recent development, the videos Bekker saw never explicitly remarked how much the furniture in Foshan would cost, but she was confident it would be far less than at the posh showrooms in London. Despite not speaking Chinese, she roamed around the furniture markets in Foshan’s warm and humid air. By the end of the trip, she had furnished her entire apartment for around £7,000 (about $9,200). Everything would go in a 20-foot container, embark from Guangzhou on a freight ship, and arrive at an English port more than two months later. Bekker’s videos attracted millions of views, and fans swarmed to the comments with the same refrain: “I have never been so influenced to go to China.”.

Four million people from over 150 countries visit Foshan’s Louvre every year to shop for furniture.

Everyone who goes to Foshan for furniture makes sure to go to the Louvre.

In the central part of Foshan, the Louvre claims to be one of the largest furniture shopping malls in China, and likely the whole world. At over 4 million square feet, it’s bigger than its namesake in France, which is the largest museum in the world; 4 million people from over 150 countries and regions visit Foshan’s Louvre every year to shop for furniture. Past the facade—which looks like an outdated convention center with blue-tinted windows and rows of country flags above the entrance—is an opulent atrium with marble columns and gilded moldings.

The complex was designed to be part of a tourist experience package, with official certification from the Chinese tourism bureau. There’s a shuttle bus from the nearest international airport and a five-star Sofitel hotel for guests. In addition to tourists from the US and Europe, there are ever more shoppers, architects, and traders from the Middle East, Africa, Russia, Central Asia, and South Asia.

Industry observers note that the Louvre contains showrooms for over 2,000 Chinese brands and 400 European ones, so there’s something for everyone. As many of these brands construct their furniture in Foshan, it’s the ideal place for a showroom. Italian minimalism is one of the most visible aesthetics here, but you’ll also find styles like Russian imperial, “fresh Chinese,” and wabi-sabi. In most places, photography is strictly prohibited to “protect original designs.”.

But the Louvre is often just a shopper’s first destination. “Foshan is not actually one furniture market. It’s a district, it’s a city, it’s an ecosystem,” notes Claudia Hofmeister, an Australia-based furniture sourcing agent who has helped clients from around the world buy furniture from Foshan; she has personally traveled there at least six times. While the Louvre is the pinnacle of luxury furniture shopping, Foshan also offers other mid-tier wholesale businesses that are 100 percent Chinese, plus lower-end furniture brands that Hofmeister says she won’t touch. “And there’s a whole lot of other models like major supercenters just dedicated to lighting, tiles, and building supplies,” she says.

For many travelers, the real shopping doesn’t happen there. The dupe factories, along with home construction and decor manufacturers, are a few miles away in Longjiang. Longjiang is known as the hub of furniture manufacturing, where you can find everything from fabrics to timber to metal parts. Its streets are lined with miles of furniture shops and nothing else. The town has its own exhibition center, but it stands in stark contrast to the opulent tourism spectacle at the Louvre.

The Louvre International Furniture Exhibition Center contains showrooms for over 2,000 Chinese brands and 400 European ones.

Every March and August, Longjiang hosts its own furniture fair, which attracts small manufacturers, dealers, and domestic buyers from other parts of China. The furniture brands in the district care less about original design and are sometimes explicit about where they draw inspiration. On the facade of a showroom building next to the exhibition center, a billboard-sized banner advertises a “Lawrence sofa,” a popular 2017 design by the famous Italian brand Minotti that can sell for over $10,000. In their booths, some sellers display portraits of a white “art director,” an Italian flag, or plaster sculptures.

Recent findings suggest that even for Chinese people, the idea of traveling to Foshan to buy furniture instead of placing orders from home is relatively latest. As China’s real estate economy slowed over the past decade, the traditional business model of licensed furniture distribution struggled. Factories now have to contend with tariffs and competition from countries where labor can be cheaper. Sourcing companies position themselves to factories as a more direct connection to consumers. Even though buyers pay to travel, they can save “30 percent to 50 percent” while still gaining access to new designs and high-quality products, states Lin Fangfang, the founder and chairman of Yueanju, one of the earliest and most influential B2C furniture sourcing agents in China.

Industry observers note that yueanju, which was founded in 2016, says it has worked closely with the local government to develop the “travel to Foshan” marketing strategy. On the radio nationwide, ads hype shopping for furniture in Foshan, with organized pickups from train stations and airports, as well as customized factory tours based on specific needs and budget. A typical three-day trip costs as little as $170 per person. Agents take care of everything and even provide a cafeteria and nap area with recliners in Yueanju’s office building in Longjiang. “Even though [Longjiang is] only one bridge away, they just won’t come here because they don’t know about us,” Lin says. “[Now], we can accommodate over 200 visitors with no problem on this floor.”.

Industry observers note that services like what Yueanju offers quickly exploded in popularity, bringing a steady flow of consumers to what had previously been a business-to-business manufacturing hub. They are now working with clients from countries including the US, Russia, Saudi Arabia, and Australia. In March, during Ramadan, the company hosted a group from Saudi Arabia. “They are royals, so their homes are pretty big,” Lin indicates. The company customized the shopping experience based on their fasting needs, only going out after 3 pm every day to preserve energy.

The modern history of furniture in Foshan started with a dupe. As the lore goes, in the 1970s a man named Li Jungang working at a carpentry factory got his hands on a couch from nearby Hong Kong, then a British colony. While upholstered furniture took off in Europe in the 17th century, traditional chairs in China were still made of hardwood and had no built-in cushioning. By the 1970s in Hong Kong, upholstered, Western-style couches were all the rage. Li cut open the couch, studied interior construction, and is said to have built what is considered the first-ever upholstered sofa in China. Similar stories citing the origin of Foshan’s relatively short history in modern furniture manufacturing are now proudly recorded in local history books, displayed in furniture showrooms, and retold by every entrepreneur in the city.

The Louvre in Foshan contains showrooms for over 2,000 Chinese brands and 400 European ones.

Italian minimalism is one of the most visible aesthetics at the Louvre, but you’ll also find styles like Russian imperial, “new Chinese,” and wabi-sabi.

It has been revealed that the rest of the story tracks the rise of manufacturing in China. As the government started embracing the market economy in the late 1970s, China became the locus of offshore manufacturing for the rest of the world. Foshan’s voracious entrepreneurs and artisans saw an opportunity to remake the city—which until then was known more for kung fu and local cuisine—into a manufacturing powerhouse. The city became known for factories that specialized in building materials, home appliances, and furniture. Foshan’s home goods industry grew to include over 7,000 businesses that account for at least one-fifth of the furniture market in China. In 2025, Foshan exported $2.65 billion worth of furniture alone. “If you have a home, you have something made in Foshan,” states the promotional slogan and industry alliance debuted by the local government in 2022.

Sources indicate that as the city became a furniture juggernaut, it developed an obsession with Italy and, more specifically, Milan, the capital of 20th-century interior design. At Salone del Mobile, the internationally renowned annual furniture fair showcasing some of the most innovative designs in the world, Foshan factory manufacturers study the latest luxury designs from Italian brands. A smaller number of companies bring their own products to the fair, and local furniture leaders also visit to help promote government collaborations between Foshan and Milan. In 2011, a Chinese newspaper reported that during that year’s furniture fair, Fendi Casa refused to admit Chinese visitors to its showroom. (Salone del Mobile did not respond to a request for comment.).

Some Foshan furniture makers do copy designs from Salone, and they do it fast. The 2026 fair ended on April 26; by May 11, Foshan furniture factories were posting on Chinese social media about mass-producing the Anywhere sofa by Edra, one of the breakout products of the year. “The first domestic fresh Anywhere sofa is here,” claims a Chinese woman in a brightly lit showroom, walking past a sofa that looks identical to the original, on Chinese social media platform Rednote. The account, under the name HY Casa, says it’s a source factory in Foshan that specializes in “high-end Italian minimal made-to-order 1:1 furniture dupes.”.

In a recent development, to create a truly convincing replica, snapping a few photos in Milan is not enough. Wang Xunyong is the owner of EIBA, a furniture brand in Foshan that produces high-end dupes of Minotti sofas by ordering the original, shipping it back to Foshan, and taking it apart to study its internal structure, just like Li did in the ’70s.

A stack of pocket springs at the EIBA factory.

EIBA is a furniture brand in Foshan that produces high-end sofa dupes.

It has been revealed that before the success of EIBA, Wang had a series of failed ventures—restaurants and several other furnishing-related businesses. Eventually, he arrived at a decision: “Instead of doing a hundred mediocre things, it’s better to take one thing to the extreme,” he states in a video posted on his social media account. In 2023, he founded his current company with a small workshop model, leveraging his past experience in the furniture business. This time, it worked.

Wang’s factory in Longjiang occupies the fourth floor of a pristine white industrial building, where a polished lobby opens into a modest showroom/workshop. Several rows of finished sofas sit near the entrance beneath ceiling spotlights. Wang has a makeshift office area that he shares with his sales staff. Every so often, a Bluetooth speaker linked to his phone announces in a flat robotic voice that someone has made a furniture order online. On the workshop floor, five or six women cut and sew sofa fabric, while several men shape foam, spray adhesive, and stretch upholstery over frames.

Wang has never been to Italy. His understanding of Italian design comes from sofas dismantled inside his factory. The first time Wang cut open an Italian-made sofa, he was struck by its complexity. It wasn’t just layers of materials stacked together, but rather a system with different densities, cutting methods, and structural logic working in harmony. He compares the sofa manufacturing process to making a cake: You can standardize the baking process by using a mold, but a complex curve would sometimes require human hands. For a long time, Wang says, many factories focused only on replicating the look of luxury couches. The proportions and silhouettes of the sofas were similar to the originals, but the internal structure was oversimplified. But that misses the essence of what makes a piece of furniture great.

Lin Qi, a factory worker, cuts paper patterns.

Zeng Xiaofeng, a factory worker, cutting fabric.

Industry observers note that this path isn’t cheap. Purchasing original pieces requires significant investment, often eight to 10 times the price of the dupes his factory produces. Once the model is thoroughly studied, efficiency improves. Today, Wang claims, his team can complete the reproduction of a fresh design within 45 days. This methodology has allowed his factory to reach annual sales of 20 million yuan (about $3 million). Unlike Minotti, which makes almost every piece of its custom furniture in Meda, Italy, Chinese factories can count on much lower costs for labor and manufacturing.

According to recent reports, to outsiders, Wang’s work is ethically dubious, but he is unapologetic. “What we’re trying to do is copy it first and surpass it later,” he says. “Many people look down on copying others, but we ignore those noises. First, we learn their details and craftsmanship. Once you have the financial strength and vision, you’ll be much better equipped to do your own thing.”.

In his view, as long as a product does not carry the original brand’s logo, it cannot be considered “counterfeit and substandard.” On a more practical level, he has developed strategies to reduce legal risk. Based on his understanding of regulations, Wang says, a piece is legally distinct if there are “seven points of difference,” even if that’s as minor as changing a board’s thickness from 3 centimeters to 2.9.

According to recent reports, wang’s rule of seven is a common belief among Chinese manufacturers, but it’s more folklore than law, claims Morgan Pietz, managing partner at the Los Angeles office of Merchant & Gould, who has represented both sides of furniture IP lawsuits. “At least under US law, there’s no rule that if you make seven changes, you are good to go,” he says.

It has been revealed that but it is difficult to legally claim that someone has knocked off a furniture design, lawyers say. In the US, most plaintiffs in the furniture industry need to go down one of two routes: Either they register patents for each of their products, or they need to demonstrate that a layperson would be able to discern the product’s origin. Both are difficult hurdles to clear. Design patents can cost around $5,000, including attorney costs and a filing fee for one product, and they only last 15 years; to make a “trade dress” claim, a furniture manufacturer needs to show that its consumers recognize the design as being from a specific source. In most cases, furniture designs don’t rise to this level of scrutiny. And no matter which route one chooses, bringing the claim to court and enforcing it could cost millions of dollars.

In a recent development, sometimes there can even be a correlation between the popularity of dupes and the sales of originals, Sprigman notes. When studying the luxury fashion knockoff industry in China, he found that buyers of counterfeit handbags can often move on to purchasing the genuine product once they become wealthier. “For some people, you could view dupes as a gateway drug to the traditional thing,” he says.

Industry observers note that to Wang, the production of dupes is not only a furniture industry phenomenon but also indicative of how capitalism in China works more broadly. “Many of our industries started from scratch. If you want results as fast as possible, you have to learn from abroad first. Whether it’s equipment, aircraft, artillery, or high-speed rail, haven’t we always followed this same path?”.

International clients select materials at the EIBA furniture factory in Foshan, China.

Sources indicate that still, creating dupes is not a business that can scale infinitely. In Wang’s view, the market for copies has become oversaturated, and competitive price wars are eating into profit margins. Foshan brands are now pivoting to original designs, not only out of ethical concerns but also due to market pressure. One day, when he has enough financial capital and experience, he hopes to develop his own designs. And only then will he consider actually traveling to Italy. Not to copy their furniture, but to experience Italian culture and find inspiration.

“You need to truly immerse yourself in that environment to feel what high-end Italian design is really about” he says.

Almost everything in Nikki Brooks’ new house came from China, which is how she got the nickname “Container Girl.” Brooks, a TikTok influencer in Texas who finds “affordable fashion” for her followers, started looking for furniture for a new home in 2024. In the past two years, she has bought windows, doors, stone countertops, tiles, beds, sofas, and even a golf cart from Chinese manufacturers, enough to fill four shipping containers.

In addition to her 150,000 followers across TikTok, Instagram, and Facebook, Brooks organized a private Facebook group where over 25,000 members discuss how to source “high-quality, cost-effective materials from overseas—especially China.” In the group, people ask each other how to import, while others share photos of their containers arriving in the US or their beautiful homes stuffed with latest purchases. Through affiliate marketing, Brooks also gets commissions from “some” products she recommends, according to her personal website.

“We’ve seen a whole crop of dupe influencers pop up, whose livelihoods are based on helping their audiences find the best deals,” says Sky Canaves, an ecommerce analyst at Emarketer, who spent over a decade reporting on China. According to Canaves, beauty and fashion influencers can take a 10 to 15 percent commission from the sales they encourage; in furniture, which is purchased less frequently, the rate can be around 5 percent, but the cost per item is higher.

While in Foshan, Bekker bought everything she needed for her upcoming apartment.

She decided to shop room by room.

In a recent development, A new generation of consumers—who came of age with Shein, Temu, and Amazon—consult TikTok or Pinterest instead of design magazines and often buy things directly through these apps. They rarely go to stores in person, if at all, and value affordability over virality. (See the Walmart Birkins, fake AirPods Max, Temu celebrity look-alikes, and everything else that’s been duped.).

Recent findings suggest that “I don’t love the term ‘dupe.’ It sounds awfully cute for something that is essentially buying a knockoff, or a counterfeit, or a theft,” says Coleman Gutshall, the vice president of strategic operations at Bernhardt Design, which develops high-end furniture with designers. From his perspective, an original piece of furniture is more expensive not because of an outrageous margin; Gutshall says his manufacturer pays fair wages for over 1,500 employees in North Carolina and works with up-and-coming designers. Many iconic pieces that are duped today were conceived of by innovative designers 50 or 100 years ago, he says, “and in order to keep that continuing, you’ve got to have this constant pipeline of designers. If they can’t make a living through loyalty and through designing, then their talent is going to waste.”.

Recent findings suggest that but not everyone in the design industry is anti-dupe. “There is no way I could ever afford an original, latest Togo sofa,” says Lauren Sinclair, an architect in New York. (A real three-seat Togo—the iconic foam-filled modular couch designed by French industrial designer Michel Ducaroy in 1973 and still handmade in France by artisans—sells for about $10,000 today.) In 2022, Sinclair paid a Chinese factory $200, plus another $700 for shipping, to get a sofa that looks just like a Togo but in a custom color and tailored to the exact size of her small New York City living room.

Recent findings suggest that “As an architect, I typically frown on dupes. I know how hard designers work to get a finished product to market and how low the margins are for bespoke furniture design,” says Sinclair, who refrains from using them in her projects. In the case of her personal dupe purchase, she argues it’s ethically acceptable because the design isn’t new. “And even if I bought an official, original Togo sofa, would that money ever go to the designer, Michel Ducaroy?” she says. “Definitely not; he died in 2009.”.

Day one would be about the living room; day two was all bedroom; bathrooms, textiles, and decor got their own time too.

On the fourth day, Bekker spent £165 on a fuzzy, round accent chair that she later learned was a copy of a piece designed by Kateryna Sokolova, an indie Ukrainian designer.

Recent findings suggest that from her deep dives on TikTok, Bekker learned about furniture agents. But she knew better: Her mother, who has an international import business and regularly travels to China, told her to always avoid the middlemen. “She had already drilled it into my head from years ago that going with an agent means they’re asking the vendor to add a commission on top every time you are making a transaction,” Bekker states. Instead, her mom arranged for a Chinese friend to drive her around Foshan on the first day. Beyond that, she had to figure out everything by herself.

Bekker planned her schedule while on her China-bound flight. She decided to shop room by room. Day one would be about the living room; day two was all bedroom; bathrooms, textiles, and decor got their own time too. She posted TikTok videos capturing what she bought: a £350 sofa, a £150 coffee table, a £50 rug, and a £80 solid-wood dining table. Bekker wasn’t explicitly hunting for dupes, but they found a way to her. On the fourth day, she spent £165 on a fuzzy, round accent chair, which she originally thought was over her budget. But the unusually high price prompted Bekker to look up the chair online through a reverse-image search. She discovered it looked exactly like a 2022 chair by Kateryna Sokolova, an indie Ukrainian designer, that sells for over £6,000 in the UK. That pushed her to purchase.

Shirley Bekker’s spontaneous furniture shopping trip to Foshan has turned into a side hustle. In July 2025, she began selling a PDF guide of her furniture purchases and their respective seller contacts on Etsy for £12.

In a recent development, ​​In the end, Bekker bought everything she needed for her fresh apartment, even down to cutlery and bedding (customized with her own logo for an additional £10). She found a warehouse in nearby Guangzhou to store all her purchases before they were shipped to London. As soon as she got home, she started using her lunch breaks to compile a spreadsheet of price comparisons, which Bekker subsequently shared in detail on TikTok: how much each purchase cost her in China and, through reverse-image search, how much a similar item would have cost in the UK.

Recent findings suggest that bekker’s spontaneous furniture shopping trip was starting to turn into a side hustle. Her followers kept asking how she found suppliers and how they could plan a trip to Foshan themselves. In July 2025, she began selling a PDF guide of her furniture purchases and their respective seller contacts on Etsy for £12. Five hundred people have bought it since, she states. In September 2025, when Bekker posted a video about receiving the container in London, followers yet again rejoiced. “It’s been MONTHS! So glad this was brought back to me,” one comment reads. Bekker has since returned to Foshan three times, toured more factories, and opened a furniture sourcing agency to plan shopping trips for international clients. The last time she was in Foshan, she ran into a follower whom she had inspired to travel to China to shop for furniture.

"It was two weeks of hammering," Vickers joked of filming the scene.

Lava-drenched and menacing, it's wholly unlike the forging of any of the other rings of power we've seen onscreen in the series so far. For showrunners McKay and J.D. Payne, that was the goal.

"We wanted it to be more than he's making a weapon or a magical object," McKay mentioned. "He's changing as a character forever. The world is changing in this moment.".

Sources indicate that in the interview, Bower and Vickers also discussed Sauron and Celeborn's surprise kiss. Plus, Robinson dug into Míriel's decision to marry Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle). Be sure to stick around until the end for Weyman's moving discussion of what it means for Gandalf to don his iconic hat for the first time. It may leave your eyes mistier than the Misty Mountains.

#116646. Latest Update: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1267 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1267 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function.
  • The findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less important than how they use that time.
  • Sources indicate that the discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function. Researchers found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the widespread assumption that screen time is necessarily harmful to developing brains.

The findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less important than how they use that time. Activities that encourage learning, creativity, and problem-solving could be particularly valuable. Researchers emphasize that the goal should not be to eliminate screen time, but to balance it with physical activity and mentally stimulating experiences.

Sources indicate that the discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers. A sedentary lifestyle has been linked to poorer academic performance, while regular exercise is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. However, scientists still have much to learn about how physical activity, sitting, and screen use during childhood influence thinking abilities later in adolescence.

These questions are especially key because childhood and adolescence are critical periods of brain development. Changes in attention, memory, and learning during these years can have lasting consequences, potentially influencing educational opportunities and career paths well into adulthood.

To investigate these relationships, Finnish researchers examined how screen time, physical activity, and sedentary behavior from childhood through adolescence were associated with cognitive performance in teenagers. They also explored whether the connections differed between boys and girls and whether the intensity of physical activity made a difference.

More Screen Time Linked to Better Thinking Skills.

One of the study's most unexpected findings was that greater screen time throughout childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.

Cognitive processing refers to the mental abilities people use to take in information, pay attention, remember details, learn fresh things, and solve problems. These abilities play an key role in school performance and everyday decision-making.

The findings challenge the idea that all screen time should be viewed as harmful. However, the researchers caution that the relationship may depend on what children are actually doing while using digital devices. Watching videos, playing games that require strategic thinking, and engaging in educational activities may involve very different levels of mental effort.

Industry observers note that "The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.

"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.

Exercise Affects Boys' and Girls' Brains Differently.

The researchers also uncovered a more complicated picture of how physical activity relates to thinking and memory.

Among girls, spending more time engaged in light-intensity physical activity since childhood was associated with better working memory during adolescence. For boys, greater participation in guided physical activity over the same period was linked to stronger working memory.

In a recent development, working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and use information. It allows someone to remember instructions while completing a task, keep track of numbers during mental calculations, or follow a conversation while processing new information.

Light-intensity physical activity generally includes relatively gentle movements that do not substantially increase breathing or heart rate. Guided physical activity refers to exercise carried out with some form of instruction or supervision, such as organized sports or structured exercise sessions.

Recent findings suggest that the differences between boys and girls suggest that the relationship between exercise and brain health may depend on more than simply how much a person moves. The type of activity, how it is organized, and the individual's sex could all play a role.

Another Surprising Finding About Physical Activity.

It has been revealed that the study produced another counterintuitive result. Teenagers who reported spending less time in unsupervised physical activity tended to perform better on measures of cognitive processing.

Yet when researchers used wearable sensors to objectively measure movement and heart rate, they found no association between overall physical activity or sedentary time and cognitive performance.

One possible explanation is that wearable devices measure movement without revealing what a person is actually doing. For example, a sensor may record periods of sitting or physical activity, but it cannot determine whether someone is solving a difficult problem, studying, participating in an organized activity, or simply resting.

This distinction could help explain why questionnaire responses revealed relationships that were not apparent in the sensor measurements.

According to recent reports, "Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.

In a recent development, "However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is important to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing.".

What the Eight-Year Study Revealed.

The findings come from an eight-year follow-up conducted as part of the PANIC study, a long-running Finnish research project investigating children's physical activity and nutrition.

It has been revealed that the current analysis included 260 participants, consisting of 124 girls and 136 boys. Their average age at the adolescent assessment was 15.8 years.

Sources indicate that researchers collected information about physical activity and sedentary behavior using both questionnaires and wearable devices that combined heart rate monitoring with movement measurements. This approach allowed them to compare participants' reported activities with data collected by sensors.

To evaluate cognitive abilities, the researchers used the CogState test battery, a collection of computerized assessments designed to measure aspects of mental performance. The tests examined learning, attention, and working memory.

According to recent reports, importantly, the findings show associations rather than cause and effect. They do not establish that increasing screen time will improve a child's thinking abilities or that reducing certain types of exercise will produce cognitive benefits. Intervention studies, in which researchers deliberately change participants' activities and measure the results, are needed to determine whether these relationships are causal.

Nevertheless, the results offer an key perspective on the continuing debate over children's screen use. Rather than treating all time spent with digital devices as equally harmful, the researchers suggest paying closer attention to whether those activities encourage active thinking and learning.

The research also highlights the importance of considering different forms of physical activity rather than focusing exclusively on the total amount of exercise children receive.

Together, the findings suggest that supporting healthy brain development may require a more nuanced approach, one that combines physical activity with opportunities for learning, creativity, and mental engagement, including those that take place on screens.

The study was published in the scientific journal Pediatric Exercise Science.

#116644. On this day in space! Nov. 23, 2015: Blue Origin sticks 1st-ever rocket landing from space with its suborbital New Shepard rocket

On this day in space! Nov. 23, 2015: Blue Origin sticks 1st-ever rocket landing from space with its suborbital New Shepard rocket

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (569 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 23, 2015, a Blue Origin rocket made a historic landing.
  • After launching the New Shepard capsule safely into space, the rocket started heading back to Earth.
  • The Blue Origin milestone meant that rockets could be reused for multiple missions, which saves money and reduces waste.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Nov. 23, 2015, a Blue Origin rocket made a historic landing. Before this time, all rockets were single-use only — even SpaceX's rockets. Blue Origin changed the concept forever.

After launching the New Shepard capsule safely into space, the rocket started heading back to Earth. It flew towards a landing pad, reignited its engine to slow down and touched down softly on the ground. This was the first successful vertical landing from space in history.

The Blue Origin milestone meant that rockets could be reused for multiple missions, which saves money and reduces waste.

Today, SpaceX may be the most well-known for landing its Falcon 9 rocket boosters from orbit. The organization's triple-core Falcon Heavy boosters can also land vertically and its massive Starship megarocket can even return to the launch site to be caught by giant metal arms.

But in the end, Blue Origin did it first.

Recent findings suggest that blue Origin's Newly introduced Shepard booster landing kicked off an era of vertical launch and vertical landings for rockets that continues to this day. It may have even outlasted the New Shepard rocket.

Since that first landing, Blue Origin has launched 17 suborbital astronaut flights with New Shepard, and 21 more uncrewed flights for a total of 38 missions between April 2015 and 2026. The company reused its New Shepard boosters repeatedly (though it did lose one during an uncrewed launch after a technical issue.) But in January 2026, the company declared a pause in New Shepard flights for two years so that it could focus on moon lander projects.

In a recent development, but Blue Origin did not abandon rocket landings. Indeed, the company's success with New Shepard led it to build vertical landing into its larger orbital rocket, New Glenn, which made its first successful landing 2025 — nearly 10 years after that first touchdown.

Blue Origin has since reflown a Fresh Glenn booster, and is developing a new rocket engine called Northstar for even better performance.

Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

#116643. Industry News: Rembrandt's 'The Night Watch' is more alive than you'd expect

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (951 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Rembrandt's 'The Night Watch' is more alive than you'd expect

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (951 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rembrandt van Rijn's "The Night Watch" is one of the most famous paintings of the Dutch Golden Age.
  • Sources indicate that in the painting, Rembrandt made dramatic use of light and shadow to guide the viewer's eye to key figures.
  • Beyond the sense of movement featured in "The Night Watch," the painting itself is also alive in a way that's rarely taken into consideration — through the microscopic organisms living on the canvas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rembrandt van Rijn's "The Night Watch" is one of the most famous paintings of the Dutch Golden Age. Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum, where the work is on display, hails the artist's 1642 masterpiece as "the turning point in his career and as the superlative example of his creative genius.".

Sources indicate that in the painting, Rembrandt made dramatic use of light and shadow to guide the viewer's eye to key figures. And unlike static group portraits typical of his era, the artist depicted Amsterdam's civic guards in mid-action, as they prepare to march out.

Beyond the sense of movement featured in "The Night Watch," the painting itself is also alive in a way that's rarely taken into consideration — through the microscopic organisms living on the canvas.

The research project "The Night Watch Lives" explores exactly that question: What kinds of life forms inhabit the surface of the famous painting?

The study is a collaborative scientific and exhibition project between the Rijksmuseum and ARTIS-Micropia — an Amsterdam museum dedicated to the world of microorganisms.

Sources indicate that it's part of the broader "Operation Night Watch" restoration and research project described as the "biggest and most wide-ranging ever study and restoration of Rembrandt's most famous painting," started in 2019. Conservators and scientists in this project have been examining every aspect of Rembrandt's masterpiece using cutting-edge technology, seeking fresh insights into its materials, condition and history — and now, its microbiome.

Sources indicate that the idea behind "The Night Watch Lives" was to "put microbes in a positive spotlight," Eline van Bloois, who led the research, told DW. "Honestly, if you're asking me — I'm a microbiologist, so I'm biased of course — but they really deserve more positive attention.".

Over a period of six months, van Bloois will be taking samples once a month directly from the famous painting at the Rijksmuseum, accompanied by the people working on the restoration of "The Night Watch.".

Using small sterile discs gently pressed against selected areas of the painting, the samples collect microscopic material from both varnished and unvarnished sections.

These samples are then cultivated in laboratories, allowing previously invisible microbes to grow into visible colonies that can be studied and identified.

Recent findings suggest that at the "The Night Watch Lives" exhibition, visitors can view Petri dishes containing the cultivated microbial colonies. A life-size reproduction of Rembrandt's masterpiece also shows where the samples were taken, and which microorganisms were found there.

Recent findings suggest that at the exhibition's opening on November 11, the installation included the findings of two of van Bloois' sampling sessions. Four more will be added over the coming months, allowing the museum's visitors to follow the results of the study as it unfolds.

That means the exhibition's visitors "will be figuring out what I've found as I'm figuring it out myself," explains the microbiologist. "We really take them through that journey with us.".

People often fear microbes or associate them with disease, even though the vast majority of these microscopic organisms are actually harmless or vital to human survival.

Some of the organisms found on the painting "are very commonly found on human skin, for instance, and they're a healthy part of the microbiome; most humans actually have these bacteria with them," claims van Bloois, adding that the presence of these microbes on the painting made sense, since humans are often near the work.

Recent findings suggest that but another bacterium stood out in the samples: Microbacterium saccharophilum, a species first identified at a sugar refinery in Japan in 2013. How this microorganism ended up on the Dutch "Night Watch," or when, is a guessing game.

Sources indicate that "It's part of the fun and part of the frustration in microbiology. You cannot ask the microbes where they originate from," claims van Bloois. "It would make our lives a bit easier, but it's also fun to have a little bit of a mystery.".

It has been revealed that the samples also revealed bacteria from soil, often found in plant roots. Could these organisms somehow harm the painting? Could plants start growing on the work?

Van Bloois explains why this is highly unlikely: On the painting, the bacteria can form inactive spores, but for the study, the researcher "provided them with all the nutrients and the right temperature and the right humidity that allowed them to grow again.".

Still, studying these organisms may eventually contribute to understanding how paintings age, how environmental conditions affect cultural heritage, and how museums can better preserve priceless works of art.

As to whether the microorganisms could date back to Rembrandt's time, the microbiologist says that's also "highly unlikely" — but here again, microbes cannot reveal their origin story.

As part of the larger "Operation Night Watch" team, van Bloois is definitely inspired by this "group effort where everyone is just really enthusiastic about telling these stories and adding to the knowledge surrounding 'The Night Watch.'".

The microbiological samples revealed by the laboratory process resemble abstract art in miniature: colorful clusters, delicate textures and intricate patterns created by living organisms.

And as the study is unfolding publicly, it also feels like an artistic performance of its own.

The project also perfectly embodies the full name of the museum where the exhibition is held: Natura Artis Magistra, a Latin phrase that translates to "nature is the teacher of art and science," as the microbiologist points out: "It's really cool to see science and art all come together in this project.".

The exhibition "The Night Watch Lives" runs at ARTIS-Micropia in Amsterdam until the end of May 2027.

#116641. Latest Update: Database Leaks Expose 3.5 Billion Usernames, Passwords, and Documents

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (915 w)

Latest Update: Database Leaks Expose 3.5 Billion Usernames, Passwords, and Documents

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (915 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • More than 3.5 billion usernames, passwords, national identity numbers, and documents were left exposed to anyone online in two unrelated databases, according to new findings shared with WIRED.
  • The findings are the latest in a seemingly endless series of revelations about incidents in which inadequately secured data puts people’s personal information at risk.
  • It has been revealed that “Personal data is personal data anywhere in the world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More than 3.5 billion usernames, passwords, national identity numbers, and documents were left exposed to anyone online in two unrelated databases, according to new findings shared with WIRED. The massive troves included data from people in dozens of countries. One seemed focused particularly on Chinese citizens and included more than a billion China-linked records.

The findings are the latest in a seemingly endless series of revelations about incidents in which inadequately secured data puts people’s personal information at risk. But the two examples also provide a window into the scale of current cybercriminal data collection—both information that attackers collect by assembling and organizing other datasets, and troves they amass using info-stealing malware.

It has been revealed that “Personal data is personal data anywhere in the world. At this point, personal data for pretty much every American is out there somewhere, and if we look at China or elsewhere, they have the same kinds of problems and security risks,” claims Greg Pollock, the director of research at security tech giant UpGuard, who found one of the exposed databases. “The cybercriminal world is reaping the benefit of decades of bad information security practices.”.

The two exposed databases are unconnected but were found at around the same time by two different researchers. Pollock’s discovery contains more than 1.5 billion aggregated documents and details of predominantly Chinese individuals and businesses. The second trove, found by Black Hills Information Security researcher Jeremiah Fowler, contains around 2 billion login credentials, with hundreds of millions linked to user accounts for mainstream United States tech platforms.

According to recent reports, exposed personal data, including usernames and passwords, has always been instrumental for scammers and cybercriminals. However, as AI cybersecurity capabilities fuel faster vulnerability exploitation, more effective scamming, and ransomware attacks, access to personal data and account credentials can be more notable than ever to attackers.

The data discovered by Pollock includes 1.64 billion documents representing personal information from at least hundreds of millions—if not around a billion—people, most of them seemingly in China based on included national ID numbers. According to his analysis, the unsecured database held at least 840 million “distinct” national ID numbers, 300 million phone numbers, around 11 million student enrollment records, and nearly 8 million business registrations. From a sample of the data, both children and deceased individuals were included in the files, Pollock indicates.

The China-linked data sat unauthenticated and openly accessible on the open internet in what seemed to be some sort of cybercriminal or gray market infrastructure. Pollock was unable to trace an owner or find contact information to notify anyone about the exposure, but as he was investigating the leak, the database became inaccessible—seemingly as part of a ransomware attack or some sort of destructive campaign. He states the database was actively being updated until the week before he discovered it.

Pollock, who has investigated data privacy and breaches for many years, claims that he attempted to validate the data during the time it was accessible, but he can’t be certain about its fidelity or whether the same trove has been circulated elsewhere. It is also possible that it contains duplicate records, though Pollock attempted to check for this. He emphasizes that it seemed like the data had been analyzed carefully for maximum value to its owner.

Recent findings suggest that “Someone had done some work to bring together a bunch of data and then normalize it to make it useful,” he notes. “There’s no legitimate source on Earth that would have all of these things structured in this way, but if you had all of these breaches and brought them together, that would be valuable to an attacker.”.

Sources indicate that the larger of the two exposed databases, found by longtime security researcher Jeremiah Fowler, contained around 2 billion credentials and appeared to be data stolen by info-stealer malware, which can collect all login details being used on an infected machine, and collections of other data from potential cybercriminal activity. There is no indication that individual companies or institutions were breached to compile the data, Fowler says.

According to recent reports, “After finding a couple of different repositories for info stealers and malware, I have a search signature to look for them,” Fowler explains to WIRED. “When this popped up, I could not believe just how massive it was.”.

Sources indicate that fowler states there were 8,471 folders in the exposed database containing plaintext credentials and account details. Some of the folders were named by country, including the US, UK, France, Germany, and dozens more. He found hundreds of millions of mainstream email accounts, tens of millions of .gov, .edu, and .org email addresses, more than 100 million social media accounts, and tens of millions of ecommerce accounts.

Sources indicate that fowler could not determine who owned the database, but he contacted the hosting manufacturer, which removed it from the internet. It’s unclear how long it was online or if anyone else accessed the information.

Industry observers note that the enormous scale of the two exposures could create a sense of hopelessness that individuals are powerless to defend their private information. And there is a public understanding about the extent of data theft across the web. But both researchers point out that after years of this escalating situation, protections like using password managers and enabling multi-factor authentication really have broadly proved effective at keeping attackers out of consumer accounts, even if they aren’t silver bullets against every kind of attack.

Breaking: Study finds slightly higher risk of autism diagnosis in areas with more lithium in drinking water, but experts say more research is needed

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 5 min read (982 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A latest study found a moderately higher risk of autism spectrum disorder in children born to pregnant people exposed to tap water with higher levels of lithium, but experts caution that this association does not show a direct link between the two.
  • About 1 in 36 children in the US is diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) each year, according to data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
  • Scientists still don’t know the exact cause of autism, a developmental disorder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A latest study found a moderately higher risk of autism spectrum disorder in children born to pregnant people exposed to tap water with higher levels of lithium, but experts caution that this association does not show a direct link between the two.

About 1 in 36 children in the US is diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) each year, according to data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Scientists still don’t know the exact cause of autism, a developmental disorder. Genetics may be a factor, but some have been looking at potential environmental causes, too.

Autism diagnosis has become more common, but pandemic disrupted early detection, CDC claims.

Cases may be on the rise, but that is also unclear. One study published this year on cases in the New York-New Jersey area found that autism diagnosis rates tripled among certain age groups between 2000 and 2016. A 2021 report found similar increases in cases, but the CDC says the increased number of cases is most likely linked to more doctors screening for the condition.

According to recent reports, lithium is an alkali metal that can be found naturally in some food and ground water. It’s used in batteries, grease and air conditioners, as well as in the treatment of bipolar disorder and some blood disorders. Its levels in US drinking water are not regulated, according to the US Geological Survey.

A new study, published Monday in the journal JAMA Pediatrics, found a small association between lithium and autism diagnosis in Denmark, where the researchers say the level of lithium in drinking water is similar to that in American water systems.

Industry observers note that the researchers checked a database of people with psychiatric disorders for children born between 2000 and 2013 to find information on 8,842 cases of ASD and 43,864 participants who did not have ASD. They then measured the concentration of lithium in 151 public waterworks that served more than half of the Danish population and mapped out where pregnant people lived in relation.

For many neurodiverse people, 'The Sims' has been a lifelong comfort.

Recent findings suggest that as lithium levels in water increased, there was a modest increased risk of an ASD diagnosis. Specifically, compared with people at the lowest exposure level, those who had the second and third highest exposure during pregnancy had a 24% to 26% higher risk of ASD diagnosed in children. The group with the highest exposure had a 46% higher risk than those at the lowest level of exposure.

The researchers could not tell how much water the pregnant people drank, but they picked Denmark in part because residents there consume some of the lowest amounts of bottled water in Europe.

Experts say it’s notable to note that the research can’t show that lithium exposure leads directly to an autism diagnosis.

Further study is required, said study co-author Dr. Beate Ritz, a professor of neurology in the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA, and a professor of epidemiology and environmental health at the UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

Sources indicate that “Any drinking water contaminants that may affect the developing human brain deserve intense scrutiny,” Ritz remarked in a news release. She added that the research would need to be replicated in other countries to look for a similar connection.

The implications of the findings are complex as far as public health policy is concerned, according to an editorial published alongside the study. Lithium levels in water, at concentrations that the study associated with a potential ASD risk, have also been linked with health benefits such as lower rates of hospitalization for psychiatric disorders and suicide.

“If all these of associations are valid, the wisdom of Solomon will be required to develop guidelines for lithium in drinking water that are maximally protective of the entire population,” wrote Dr. David C. Bellinger, a professor of neurology and psychology at Harvard Medical School. “Until the basic biology of ASD is better understood, it will be difficult to distinguish causal from spurious associations.”.

'Heartbreaking' delays in autism diagnosis and treatment got even worse during pandemic.

Dr. Max Wiznitzer, director of the Rainbow Autism Center at University Hospitals Rainbow Babies and Children’s Hospital in Cleveland, points to other research on the effects of lithium on pregnant people who take it for mental health disorders. Those studies – which look at people exposed to much higher levels than are found in drinking water – do not show a connection with autism spectrum disorder.

“It’s an interesting association, but causation is definitely not proven,” said Wiznitzer, who was not involved in the new research. “We have to see if there’s a viable and biologically plausible mechanism by which a small amount of lithium in the water supply can somehow do this, yet pharmacologic dosing of lithium in women with bipolar disorder has not been reported to be causing increased risk of ASD.”.

In a recent development, other studies have also suggested connections between ASD and environmental exposures to things like pesticides, air pollution and phthalates. But none of them points to any of these factors as a direct cause of the disorder.

Sources indicate that A link between environmental exposure and ASD is hard to prove, Wiznitzer stated. With research showing that increased exposure to air pollution raises the risk of giving birth to a child with ASD, for example, he often wonders whether pollution is the determining factor or if it’s just the populations who live in more polluted areas.

According to recent reports, “There’s a lot of speculation about about environmental factors, but how many of them are truly causally associated?” Wiznitzer remarked. “We are bombarded with a variety of environmental stressors in our everyday lives. We have to figure out how to basically safely navigate them, and this is probably not one that’s high on our list.”.
